articles.title: Keiko Fujimori sobre fenómeno El Niño: “Se vienen tiempos difíciles (...) afecta al mundo pero al Perú lo va a golpear mucho más fuerte”
articles.summary: La presidenta de la República, Keiko Fujimori, advirtió que el Perú afrontará épocas difíciles por los efectos del fenómeno El Niño. La mandataria señaló que el calentamiento de las aguas marinas impacta de forma directa en las actividades productivas de la costa nacional.
articles.body_text: La presidenta de la República, Keiko Fujimori, advirtió que el Perú afrontará épocas difíciles por los efectos del fenómeno El Niño. La mandataria señaló que el calentamiento de las aguas marinas impacta de forma directa en las actividades productivas de la costa nacional. “Se vienen tiempos difíciles, no podemos negarlo. El fenómeno El Niño es un fenómeno climatológico que está afectando al mundo, pero que al Perú lo va a golpear mucho más fuerte”, señaló esta mañana. La mandataria remarcó que las actuales condiciones restringen la temporada de extracción de anchoveta en todo el territorio. El cambio en el océano redujo la presencia de este recurso tradicional y favoreció la llegada de especies alternativas. “Ya estamos viendo algunos de sus efectos pero los peruanos somos resilientes, los peruanos no nos rendimos y hemos sabido siempre ponernos de pie frente a las peores dificultades, pero eso se ha conseguido cuando se trabajo en equipo”, destacó. Fujimori afirmó que el golpe económico será severo para los sectores vinculados a la actividad marítima. Ante este panorama, la gobernante pidió a la ciudadanía firmeza y unidad para encarar las consecuencias del evento climático. En las primeras horas del día, Keiko Fujimori visitó el buque científico Humboldt en la bahía del Callao para el lanzamiento del recetario Mar de Oportunidades. El ministro de la Producción, Juan Carlos Requejo, acompañó a la mandataria en la presentación de opciones culinarias con pota y cachema. Durante la cita oficial, la mandataria entregó platos de reconocimiento a chefs nacionales y saludó la labor de las madres de comedores populares. Asimismo, Fujimori fijó la meta gubernamental de reducir la prevalencia de la anemia infantil de 40% a 20% mediante estos alimentos marinos.

articles.title: Huracán Simón de categoría 4 EN VIVO | nueva trayectoria, cuándo y dónde tocará tierra en México
articles.summary: El lento desplazamiento del huracán Simón frente a Jalisco amenaza con prolongar los efectos más severos en la costa de México, con vientos de hasta 230 km/h, olas de nueve metros y lluvias extraordinarias
articles.body_text: Los últimos pronósticos del domingo redujeron las posibilidades de que el huracán Simón toque tierra en México, sin que disminuyan los riesgos de fuertes lluvias y vientos severos. El ciclón avanza a un ritmo peligrosamente lento y paralelo a la costa del Pacífico en una categoría 4 de 5 en la escala Saffir Simpson. Los efectos suelen golpear más a medida que pasa más tiempo en un mismo lugar. Pero “parece estar sintiendo los efectos del terreno alto” de la cadena montañosa que atraviesa esta región, indicó la agencia de huracanes de Estados Unidos (NHC) en su boletín más reciente. El NHC observó que es “cada vez más probable que Simón evite tocar tierra directamente a corto plazo”. El gobierno mexicano prevé “que se debilite paulatinamente durante las próximas horas”, según su último reporte. Un equipo de la AFP fue a Puerto Vallarta, una joya turística que será golpeada por los efectos del huracán. Las autoridades piden a los paseantes alejarse del malecón. Las olas rompían con fuerza sobre este paseo y el agua rebasaba una estatua de un caballito de mar de unos dos metros. “Ven la ola y parece que les dicen arrímense (acérquense)”, reprochó una policía sobre un grupo de turistas que se acerca a tomar fotos e ignora la indicación de alejarse de la orilla. “Vemos a varias personas que les cuesta un poco acatar indicaciones y se ponen en riesgo”, indicó la oficial Claudia Matías. Los negocios protegieron ventanas y puertas con tablones, y en algunos pintaron en aerosol mensajes como “Simón dice: ‘todo va a estar bien’”, en referencia al popular juego en el que los niños siguen instrucciones, o “Simón, sé breve, pacífico” junto al dibujo de un tiburón y caras felices. Manuel Jaime, habitante de Vallarta de 37 años, caminaba en la acera de enfrente, llena de negocios tapiados. Salió a pasear con su familia para relajarse. “En esta ocasión parece ser que va a estar muy tranquilo el puerto, esperemos que sí”, dijo. Pero la intensidad de la lluvia y la marea incrementa hacia la tarde. Vicente García, un turista de 48 años, proveniente de California, coincide. “Esperábamos una tormenta más grande ayer, así que permanecimos adentro, pero me alegra que no fuera así”, indicó. “Ya nos vamos mañana”. Por la mañana el gobierno mexicano estimó que hacia las 18H00 locales del domingo el centro del ciclón llegaría a unos 15 km de las costas del estado de Jalisco. Aunque no toque tierra “todas las bandas nubosas del ciclón o la parte intensa del ciclón de todos modos va a estar afectando” poblados a la orilla del mar, explicó a la AFP el director del servicio meteorológico de México, Fabián Vázquez. “Vamos a tener efectos muy severos sobre todo de viento en la costa” con olas de hasta nueve metros y lluvias extraordinarias, añadió. El sábado, la Marina de México evacuó por barco a un centenar de personas de poblados costeros amenazados por Simón. En Puerto Vallarta, decenas de habitantes comenzaron a llegar a los refugios provenientes de colonias en riesgo por inundaciones. “A lo mejor si llega el huracán, va a levantar la casa y por eso mejor decidimos venir a un refugio”, dice José de Jesús Santillán, albañil de 55 años, sentado en un camastro. En otro albergue permanece Raquel García, de 58 años. Vive en una zona de riesgo por inundaciones. Pero no le preocupan demasiado las pérdidas materiales. “Con el tiempo, lo vamos a recuperar (...) yo prefiero mi vida y la de mi esposo que las cosas”.

articles.title: Fenómeno El Niño: Keiko Fujimori inspecciona obras de prevención ante inundaciones y huaicos en Piura y La Libertad
articles.summary: Keiko Fujimori supervisa obras preventivas ante El Niño en Piura y La Libertad. Conoce los avances, la inversión y las zonas que serían beneficiadas.
articles.body_text: La presidenta de la República, Keiko Fujimori, supervisa este viernes las obras de prevención ante el fenómeno El Niño en las regiones de Piura y La Libertad. La mandataria realiza la visita junto con el ministro de Desarrollo Agrario y Riego, Marco Vinelli, y el ministro de Defensa, Rafael Belaúnde, para verificar los avances de las intervenciones destinadas a reducir el riesgo de inundaciones y huaicos. La jornada forma parte del viaje de trabajo número 21 de la jefa de Estado y comprende la inspección de trabajos de limpieza y descolmatación de cauces, la conformación de bordos y las obras de protección en puntos críticos de ambas regiones. En Piura, Fujimori supervisará las intervenciones ejecutadas por la Autoridad Nacional del Agua (ANA), que incluyen la limpieza, descolmatación y conformación de bordos para facilitar el desplazamiento del agua ante eventuales crecidas. Uno de los sectores con mayor avance es Los Ejidos–Puente Bolognesi, donde los trabajos alcanzaron el 100% de ejecución física: se intervinieron los 4,85 kilómetros previstos. Sin embargo, el avance en volumen de descolmatación llega al 85,30%, equivalente a 464.382 metros cúbicos. En otros puntos, las labores continúan en ejecución. El sector El Milagro–La Encantada registra un avance físico del 27,59%, mientras que Piedra Negra alcanza el 20,73%. Las autoridades también verificarán las intervenciones a cargo del Ministerio de Defensa en siete sectores de la región. Estas acciones forman parte de las medidas preventivas previstas para mejorar la capacidad de los cauces de ríos y quebradas frente a posibles incrementos del caudal. En el marco del Decreto de Urgencia N.° 008-2026, se programaron 21 intervenciones en Piura, con una meta conjunta de 49,35 kilómetros de cauces de ríos y quebradas. Los trabajos buscan reducir la acumulación de sedimentos y mejorar las condiciones para el tránsito del agua, con el objetivo de disminuir los riesgos de desbordes e inundaciones durante el fenómeno El Niño. Según la información proporcionada, la culminación de las labores en Los Ejidos–Puente Bolognesi está prevista para el 18 de octubre de 2026. La supervisión permitirá verificar el estado de las intervenciones y el cumplimiento de los plazos establecidos. En La Libertad, la presidenta realizará un sobrevuelo para verificar el progreso de la solución integral de las quebradas San Ildefonso y San Carlos, proyecto ejecutado por la Autoridad Nacional de Infraestructura (ANIN). De acuerdo con el reporte técnico proporcionado, las obras presentan avances físicos de 78,82% en San Ildefonso y 69,52% en San Carlos. La inversión total asciende a S/ 1.664 millones. El proyecto contempla la construcción de diques, un túnel de 1,5 kilómetros para derivar las aguas de la quebrada San Ildefonso hacia San Carlos, canales de conducción que suman 12,85 kilómetros y defensas ribereñas a lo largo de 17,2 kilómetros del río Moche. Estas infraestructuras buscan encauzar las aguas y reducir la exposición de las zonas urbanas y productivas ante eventuales lluvias intensas y huaicos.

articles.title: Jauja: techo colapsa por vientos fuertes y deja una persona fallecida y tres heridas
articles.summary: En Jauja, techo colapsa Un fatal accidente ocurrió luego que cayera el techo del coliseo comunal del distrito de Canchayllo, en la provincia de Jauja, dejando como saldo un muerto y tres heridospor vientos fuertes y deja una fallecida y tres heridas.
articles.body_text: Un fatal accidente ocurrió luego que cayera el techo del coliseo comunal del distrito de Canchayllo, en la provincia de Jauja, dejando como saldo un muerto y tres heridos. El hecho ocurrió frente a 200 pobladores mientras celebraran el aniversario de la localidad. La Agencia Andina indicó que estructura metálica, las calaminas y parte de los troncos de madera cedieron ante la fuerza del viento y cayeron sobre un grupo de asistentes que participaba en un almuerzo ofrecido por la comunidad campesina. La persona fallecida fue identificada como Juana Poves Michue, de 74 años. Pese a haber sido trasladada al hospital Domingo Olavegoya de Jauja, falleció a causa de la severidad de sus heridas. El resto de heridos responden al nombre de Olinda Poves y el ingeniero Joel Recuay, quienes fueron llevados de emergencia junto a otras víctimas a hospital jaujino. También se reportó niños heridos. Al ver lo ocurrido, más de 50 cadetes de la Escuela de Suboficiales de Pilcomayo que se encontraban cerca del lugar acudieron a socorrer a los contusos y colaborar con el traslado de los heridos. Minutos despues, tras confirmarse la gravedad del accidente, el alcalde José Espinoza Vásquez suspendió de inmediato todas las actividades del aniversario distrital para acompañar en el dolor a las familias de la víctima mortal y los lesionados.

articles.title: Keiko Fujimori sobre fenómeno El Niño: “Se vienen tiempos difíciles (...) afecta al mundo pero al Perú lo va a golpear mucho más fuerte”
articles.summary: La presidenta de la República, Keiko Fujimori, advirtió que el Perú afrontará épocas difíciles por los efectos del fenómeno El Niño. La mandataria señaló que el calentamiento de las aguas marinas impacta de forma directa en las actividades productivas de la costa nacional.
articles.body_text: La presidenta de la República, Keiko Fujimori, advirtió que el Perú afrontará épocas difíciles por los efectos del fenómeno El Niño. La mandataria señaló que el calentamiento de las aguas marinas impacta de forma directa en las actividades productivas de la costa nacional. “Se vienen tiempos difíciles, no podemos negarlo. El fenómeno El Niño es un fenómeno climatológico que está afectando al mundo, pero que al Perú lo va a golpear mucho más fuerte”, señaló esta mañana. La mandataria remarcó que las actuales condiciones restringen la temporada de extracción de anchoveta en todo el territorio. El cambio en el océano redujo la presencia de este recurso tradicional y favoreció la llegada de especies alternativas. “Ya estamos viendo algunos de sus efectos pero los peruanos somos resilientes, los peruanos no nos rendimos y hemos sabido siempre ponernos de pie frente a las peores dificultades, pero eso se ha conseguido cuando se trabajo en equipo”, destacó. Fujimori afirmó que el golpe económico será severo para los sectores vinculados a la actividad marítima. Ante este panorama, la gobernante pidió a la ciudadanía firmeza y unidad para encarar las consecuencias del evento climático. En las primeras horas del día, Keiko Fujimori visitó el buque científico Humboldt en la bahía del Callao para el lanzamiento del recetario Mar de Oportunidades. El ministro de la Producción, Juan Carlos Requejo, acompañó a la mandataria en la presentación de opciones culinarias con pota y cachema. Durante la cita oficial, la mandataria entregó platos de reconocimiento a chefs nacionales y saludó la labor de las madres de comedores populares. Asimismo, Fujimori fijó la meta gubernamental de reducir la prevalencia de la anemia infantil de 40% a 20% mediante estos alimentos marinos.

articles.title: Huracán Simón de categoría 4 EN VIVO | nueva trayectoria, cuándo y dónde tocará tierra en México
articles.summary: El lento desplazamiento del huracán Simón frente a Jalisco amenaza con prolongar los efectos más severos en la costa de México, con vientos de hasta 230 km/h, olas de nueve metros y lluvias extraordinarias
articles.body_text: Los últimos pronósticos del domingo redujeron las posibilidades de que el huracán Simón toque tierra en México, sin que disminuyan los riesgos de fuertes lluvias y vientos severos. El ciclón avanza a un ritmo peligrosamente lento y paralelo a la costa del Pacífico en una categoría 4 de 5 en la escala Saffir Simpson. Los efectos suelen golpear más a medida que pasa más tiempo en un mismo lugar. Pero “parece estar sintiendo los efectos del terreno alto” de la cadena montañosa que atraviesa esta región, indicó la agencia de huracanes de Estados Unidos (NHC) en su boletín más reciente. El NHC observó que es “cada vez más probable que Simón evite tocar tierra directamente a corto plazo”. El gobierno mexicano prevé “que se debilite paulatinamente durante las próximas horas”, según su último reporte. Un equipo de la AFP fue a Puerto Vallarta, una joya turística que será golpeada por los efectos del huracán. Las autoridades piden a los paseantes alejarse del malecón. Las olas rompían con fuerza sobre este paseo y el agua rebasaba una estatua de un caballito de mar de unos dos metros. “Ven la ola y parece que les dicen arrímense (acérquense)”, reprochó una policía sobre un grupo de turistas que se acerca a tomar fotos e ignora la indicación de alejarse de la orilla. “Vemos a varias personas que les cuesta un poco acatar indicaciones y se ponen en riesgo”, indicó la oficial Claudia Matías. Los negocios protegieron ventanas y puertas con tablones, y en algunos pintaron en aerosol mensajes como “Simón dice: ‘todo va a estar bien’”, en referencia al popular juego en el que los niños siguen instrucciones, o “Simón, sé breve, pacífico” junto al dibujo de un tiburón y caras felices. Manuel Jaime, habitante de Vallarta de 37 años, caminaba en la acera de enfrente, llena de negocios tapiados. Salió a pasear con su familia para relajarse. “En esta ocasión parece ser que va a estar muy tranquilo el puerto, esperemos que sí”, dijo. Pero la intensidad de la lluvia y la marea incrementa hacia la tarde. Vicente García, un turista de 48 años, proveniente de California, coincide. “Esperábamos una tormenta más grande ayer, así que permanecimos adentro, pero me alegra que no fuera así”, indicó. “Ya nos vamos mañana”. Por la mañana el gobierno mexicano estimó que hacia las 18H00 locales del domingo el centro del ciclón llegaría a unos 15 km de las costas del estado de Jalisco. Aunque no toque tierra “todas las bandas nubosas del ciclón o la parte intensa del ciclón de todos modos va a estar afectando” poblados a la orilla del mar, explicó a la AFP el director del servicio meteorológico de México, Fabián Vázquez. “Vamos a tener efectos muy severos sobre todo de viento en la costa” con olas de hasta nueve metros y lluvias extraordinarias, añadió. El sábado, la Marina de México evacuó por barco a un centenar de personas de poblados costeros amenazados por Simón. En Puerto Vallarta, decenas de habitantes comenzaron a llegar a los refugios provenientes de colonias en riesgo por inundaciones. “A lo mejor si llega el huracán, va a levantar la casa y por eso mejor decidimos venir a un refugio”, dice José de Jesús Santillán, albañil de 55 años, sentado en un camastro. En otro albergue permanece Raquel García, de 58 años. Vive en una zona de riesgo por inundaciones. Pero no le preocupan demasiado las pérdidas materiales. “Con el tiempo, lo vamos a recuperar (...) yo prefiero mi vida y la de mi esposo que las cosas”.

articles.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.
articles.body_text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly. Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back. Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models.

articles.title: Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery.
articles.body_text: Maybe it was the grey color, the slightly bulbous roofline, or the vaguely SUV-like proportions of the electric Porsche Macan, but as I shuttled kids and groceries around city and suburban streets, I never once noticed a longing stare from other drivers. Unlike with other cars I’ve tested, no enthusiasts stopped to ask me questions. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo simply blended in, leaving in its wake a raft of existential questions. What is a sports car, anyway? Does it need to be overwhelmingly extroverted? Should it match the leaner, lighter look of its gas-powered sibling? Drive one and the questions cease. Maybe that’s because the acceleration makes it hard to breathe? Or maybe it’s because, by the numbers, the Macan is a sports car at heart despite its rather humdrum crossover body style. My passengers would agree. The kids I drove to soccer practice, both my own and others, gave the punchy acceleration high marks. The G-forces it reports on the head-up display ($2,660) can easily mimic the pull of gravity. Stab the accelerator at 70 mph and it lurches as though it were standing still. (Don’t worry, fellow parents. I did not try that with children on board.) On winding roads, the car comes alive, thanks in part to the four-wheel steering ($2,150). Drop it into Sport Plus mode, and the car literally drops on its air suspension. Are we sure this is another anonymous crossover? Maybe anonymity is a useful trait in a car this responsive and powerful. Unlike most two-row crossovers, you get the feeling of sitting in the Macan, not on it. The wheel extends far enough to make a sporty driving position possible, and the classic Porsche chronometer ($1,040) perched atop the dash ticks off the seconds it takes to get the kid to soccer practice. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. The EV, which the automaker provided to me for a week, starts at $112,700. However, the one I drove rang up at $149,610, including destination fees. Yes, the options alone could buy a nicely equipped Chevy Bolt . With Porsche and options, if you have to ask…well, it’s better not to. The Porsche Macan Turbo EV I drove came in Slate Grey Neo (a $2,620 upgrade), which was really well executed and among the best greys I’ve seen. If you crave luxurious anonymity, then this grey is your color. There were a slew of other options, and in my view, not all of them are worth it. I’d skip the passenger display ($1,710); my kids liked that it could play YouTube videos, but they can’t ride up front, and my wife was underwhelmed. “Our washing machine can play YouTube videos,” she said. I’d also forgo the illuminated Porsche wordmark on the front seatbacks ($690), puddle lamps that shine “PORSCHE” onto the pavement ($420), Porsche crests on the headrests ($640), and an illuminated Turbo badge on the door sills ($1,230). That Turbo badge became a point of contention for some of my friends, who were quick to point out that EVs technically can’t have turbos. That is true, though automotive names have long been divorced from reality. Almost every Porsche these days has a turbo, even those not labeled as such. It’s not just Porsche: BMW’s model numbers, for example, stopped reflecting engine displacement decades ago, and the Ford Galaxie never traveled between star systems using its hyperdrive. Sorry, friends, I’m not taking the bait.

articles.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles.
articles.body_text: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. articles.title: Waymo's robotaxis are headed to Canada | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The company will start off by testing its self-driving vehicles on Toronto's streets.
articles.body_text: Alphabet’s self-driving car unit, Waymo, is expanding into Canada after receiving approval to participate in Ontario’s automated vehicle pilot program. The company isn’t launching a robotaxi service just yet, though. Waymo tends to follow the same playbook for every new city, gradually proceeding from manual mapping to testing, and eventually operating a commercial service. Waymo said in a blog post on Friday that its self-driving vehicles will be manually driven in Toronto to create high-definition maps of local street networks. The company will then test its autonomous vehicles on public roads with a human safety operator on board. These operators will eventually be pulled from the driver’s seat, and afterwards the company will invite the public to take rides in its robotaxis. Waymo’s move into Canada is part of an aggressive push into new markets that’s picking up speed. Two years ago, the company was operating in only three commercial markets, and its robotaxis were not yet driving on freeways. Its expansion plans kicked off in March 2025 with a deployment in Austin, and later in Atlanta. Today, the company has robotaxi services in 15 U.S. cities, and is testing them in London and Tokyo as well. The company’s co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the expansion into Canada marks an important milestone in its global journey. This is also the northernmost and possibly most wintry city that Waymo has so far tried to operate in, so these conditions will test its AV technology and operational savviness. As part of its accelerated expansion strategy, Waymo has started partnering with third-party companies to manage its fleet in each respective city. Toronto is no different: Waymo said it has partnered with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, and expects to support hundreds of jobs in spaces such as fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and operations. articles.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them | TechCrunch
articles.summary: According to Elorian's evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
articles.body_text: Elorian , the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The model, Glimpse , is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface is waitlist-only, so for now it’s a results table and a thesis. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see. Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw. For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night. Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.” “Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said. The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against. Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna. But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks. Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean. The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test. articles.title: In 'You Can See Everything,' Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nathan Fielder's documentary about disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes has created a constellation of colliding personas that interrogate the very nature of authenticity.
articles.body_text: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” [The rest of this review contains spoilers.] Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up.

articles.title: Tressfecta wants to make hair braiding a less arduous task for hairstylists | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Tressfecta builds products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins.
articles.body_text: Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own. “Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns. At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream. Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding. “It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.” Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies. She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday , she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said. articles.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes, known as "superfakes," as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
articles.body_text: Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “ superfakes ,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods. Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app. Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link. “Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said. The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass. “The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.” This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified. The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story. The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine. Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops. Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon . articles.title: Replit's CEO says the future of work is the 'self-driving company' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad envisions a future of “self-driving companies,” where AI agents handle day-to-day tasks and people focus on higher-level decisions.
articles.body_text: Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them. He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste. “The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said. He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year. “Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.” Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed. And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent. “You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained. The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on. “We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.” He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.) “There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

articles.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Benchmark says the Valley’s rule against backing rivals is getting harder to keep.
articles.body_text: For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule. It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies. Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10- to 15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference. “The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.” Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.” Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.” He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said. Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added. Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid. articles.title: Elon Musk tells advertisers: “Go fuck yourself”
articles.summary: Elon Musk said that the X ad boycott could kill his company, but he told advertisers to “stop” instead of trying to “blackmail me.”
articles.body_text: Elon Musk took the stage at the DealBook conference on Wednesday evening with nervous laughter and a cascade of jokes about himself and his companies. But the interview quickly turned to the more serious subject of Musk’s recent antisemitic posts on X (formerly Twitter) and whether his company can survive the advertiser boycott. On that matter, Musk seemed alternatingly apologetic and defiant — acknowledging his mistakes, then doing everything in his power to push advertisers away. “I hope they stop. Don’t advertise,” Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin. “If somebody is going to try to blackmail me with advertising, blackmail me with money, go fuck yourself. Go fuck yourself. Is that clear? I hope it is.” He singled out Disney CEO Bob Iger, who discussed not wanting Disney to be affiliated with Musk while onstage earlier in the day. “Hey Bob, if you’re in the audience.” If advertisers don’t return, Musk said, “what this advertising boycott is going to do is it’s going to kill the company.” He seemed almost resigned to the possibility, speaking of it almost as though X were a martyr and advertisers the enemy. “That is what everybody on Earth will know,” he said. “We’ll be gone, and it’ll be gone because of an advertiser boycott.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U_M_uvDChJQ] Musk’s message to advertisers came after what had briefly appeared to be an attempt to salvage the damage he caused after he called an antisemitic post the “actual truth” two weeks ago. More than 100 brands have since halted their ads, and the company is at risk of losing $75 million by the end of the year, according to The New York Times. “I should in retrospect should not have replied to that one person,” Musk said. He blamed media outlets for not covering his clarifications before apologizing. “Essentially I handed a loaded gun to those who hate me, and arguably to those are antisemitic, and for that I’m quite sorry. That was not my intention.” But even in his attempts to explain himself — that out of tens of thousands of posts on X, he’s bound to say “foolish” things — Musk insisted he wasn’t on an “apology tour.” He said his recent visit to Israel wasn’t in response to the criticism of his posts and that he didn’t mind being an object of contempt. He then went on a rambling explanation of what he says he really meant: his belief that Jewish people are funding causes meant to “annihilate” them. His attempted clarification only seemed to further the antisemitic conspiracy theory he promoted in the first place, broadly blaming “people in the Jewish community” for their support of unnamed activist groups. X CEO Linda Yaccarino — the former advertising chief at NBCUniversal who Musk brought on board to shore up the platform’s appeal to advertisers — took to X shortly after her CTO’s rant to say this: “Here’s my perspective when it comes to advertising: X is standing at a unique and amazing intersection of Free Speech and Main Street — and the X community is powerful and is here to welcome you. To our partners who believe in our meaningful work — Thank You.” The full interview was meandering and at times devolved into stream of consciousness responses; Musk spoke for triple the time most other interviewees did. But the questions around Musk’s own actions, and the resulting advertiser exodus — the things that could materially impact X — seemed to garner the most nonchalant answers. He doesn’t seem to care. Update November 30th, 4:35AM ET: Added statement from X CEO Linda Yaccarino.

articles.title: Another major ad agency recommends pausing Twitter ad campaigns
articles.summary: Omnicom Media Group recommended that clients (which include Pepsi, Apple, and McDonald’s) pause advertising on Twitter, citing “potential serious implications” since Elon Musk’s takeover. It’s the second of the “big four” agencies to do so, following IPG.
articles.body_text: Omnicom, one of the world’s biggest ad firms, representing brands like McDonald’s, Apple, and PepsiCo, is recommending clients pause spending on Twitter, according to an internal memo obtained by The Verge. Omnicom Media Group is recommending clients “pause activity on Twitter in the short term,” according to a note titled “Twitter - Continued Brand Safety Concerns.” The memo cites recent events in the last few days that have “potential serious implications” for brands running ads on the platform. The memo cites the deep layoffs of Twitter trust and safety teams, the resignations of high-profile executives, and the slew of “verified” impersonation accounts as being key issues for advertisers. There is “evidence that the risk to our clients’ brand safety has risen sharply to a level most would find unacceptable,” the memo reads. “We recommend pausing activity on Twitter in the short term until the platform can prove it has reintroduced safeguards to an acceptable level and has regained control of its environment.” The memo goes on to say that Omnicom has “formally requested that Twitter assure us that these issues will not impact compliant processes, operations, products, brand safety and client investment on the platform in any way” but that “seemingly due to the lack of senior leadership now in these areas, Twitter has not been able to give those assurances.” It’s the latest in a string of advertisers that have changed plans following the chaos at Twitter since Elon Musk’s takeover. Last week, IPG, another ad agency giant, recommended its clients suspend their advertising on Twitter, according to CNBC. Companies like Volkswagen, General Motors, and General Mills have also pulled ad spending from Twitter in recent weeks. The majority of Twitter’s revenue comes from ads, and despite Musk’s questionable efforts at soothing their concerns, advertisers are worried about their content showing up next to an influx of hate speech and impersonations. They’re also concerned about Musk’s own tweets, like his threats to “thermonuclear name & shame” advertisers who pull their money from the platform. In Musk’s first email to Twitter employees, the billionaire owner said roughly half of the company’s revenue would need to come from subscriptions. But in the last few days, Twitter Blue, the premium tier for $7.99 a month that Musk has been pushing, has been through tumultuous changes in the short time it’s been live. As of writing, Twitter Blue has been suspended just days after the rushed launch — though who’s to say that won’t change in an hour.

The moral bankruptcy of Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz
articles.summary: Two of the most famous investors in Silicon Valley endorsed Donald Trump. This is less about tech generally than their investment portfolio, specifically.
articles.body_text: Last week, the founders of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz declared their allegiance to Donald Trump in their customary fashion: talking about money on a podcast. “Sorry, Mom,” Ben Horowitz says in an episode of The Ben & Marc Show. “I know you’re going to be mad at me for this. But, like, we have to do it.” Marc Andreessen and Horowitz insist they voted for Democrats until now. They are friends with liberals. They claim to be nervous about the social blowback they will receive for this, especially because of the historically progressive nature of the tech industry and the Bay Area. But given the general movement among their class toward Trump, I think those claims about being nervous are overblown, if not performative. There is, for instance, Elon Musk’s pro-Trump super PAC, which has support from Sequoia Capital’s Shaun Maguire and 8VC’s Joe Lonsdale, among other notables. (The Wall Street Journal reported Musk is planning to donate $45 million a month, which Musk has denied.) There’s the $160 million the crypto movement has put forward in support of crypto-friendly candidates. We can’t forget their VC pal David Sacks speaking at the Republican National Convention. And last but not least, there’s Trump’s running mate choice of JD Vance, a former venture capitalist whose firm’s investors included Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt, and Andreessen himself. This isn’t a movement. It’s a clique. The podcast itself is an extraordinary performance. At one point, Andreessen concedes that their major problems with President Joe Biden — the ones that led them to support Trump — are what most voters would consider “subsidiary” issues. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the big issues that people care about,” he says. If we take this podcast at face value, we are to believe that these subsidiary issues are the only reason they’ve chosen to endorse and donate to Trump. These subsidiary issues take precedence for Andreessen and Horowitz over, say, mass deportations and Project 2025’s attempt to end no-fault divorce. We are looking at a simple trade against personal liberty — abortion, the rights of gay and trans people, and possibly democracy itself — in favor of crypto, AI, and a tax policy they like better. For Horowitz, “probably the most emotional topic” is crypto — a16z started a $4.5 billion crypto fund in 2022, and the pair believe that the Biden administration has been deeply unfair to crypto. In Horowitz’s view, the Biden administration “basically subverted the rule of law to attack the crypto industry.” Certainly much of the crypto industry prefers Trump. But it seems obvious that there has been a lot of intra-agency squabbling as Congress dithered on passing any laws. To place the blame squarely on Biden is bizarre, particularly when we have Trump’s chaotic previous term as guidance. Sure, Trump is no longer saying Bitcoin is “a scam against the dollar,” as he did in 2021; he is scheduled to speak at the Bitcoin conference this year. But his record in office is not exactly pro-crypto. During the Trump administration, financial regulator FinCEN initially asked the public to provide comments on a crypto rule change over a 15-day period that included Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day, which effectively shortened the comment window by four working days. There is also the Ripple Labs enforcement case, in which the SEC is seeking a $1.95 billion fine; it, too, dates to the Trump administration. The pair’s complaints about Gary Gensler, the current head of the Securities and Exchange Commission, are striking. They are particularly annoyed that he won’t pay attention to them. “We’re the largest crypto investors or largest blockchain investors in the world, and we’ve requested meetings with him at least a half a dozen times,” Horowitz says. Gensler has not met with them. Neither, they say, has Senator Elizabeth Warren or Biden himself. In fact, Andreessen makes it clear that he expects presidential attention, something he’s been getting since he was 23. Given the number of times Andreessen and Horowitz make references to various meetings with various politicians, it’s easy to get the impression that they are mostly insulted that they are being treated like ordinary constituents. From crypto, we move to AI, which Andreessen and Horowitz don’t think is being regulated correctly either. According to Horowitz, AI is as powerful as, or more powerful than, the internet and the global computer industry from the 1950s on. “This may be the biggest technological boom of all time,” Andreessen says. Andreessen says in his newsletter-cum-manifesto, “The Little Tech Agenda,” that he is worried that AI will face similar scrutiny to crypto. The FTC has issued guidance to the AI industry that indicated it will pursue companies that exaggerate what their AI can do, say they are using AI when they are not, and recklessly put products on the market without properly analyzing the risks. Meanwhile, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has told lenders that they must supply a reason for a credit denial that’s better than just “computer says no” when using AI models. These regulations have little to do with technology and a lot to do with old-fashioned lying. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz single out Biden’s executive order about artificial intelligence. The order requires companies to disclose the presence of very large models, as well as to provide the government information about what the plans are for the model, what cybersecurity measures are taken to protect those models, and the results of red-team testing for sensitive subjects, among other things. This is in keeping with Horowitz’s assertion about the seriousness of the technology. So what’s the problem? The two focus on computing power. The disclosure requirements apply to “any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 1023 integer or floating-point operations.” Andreessen and Horowitz think specifying such a limit is ridiculous. Little tech “will be snuffed out by this kind of regulation,” Horowitz says. It is perhaps worth noting that nothing above the size specified in the executive order — the size Andreessen and Horowitz object to — even exists yet, according to Arati Prabhakar, Biden’s top tech advisor. The fundamental complaint here is that these two believe that the Biden administration’s approach to AI “enshrine[s] the two or three companies that they believe are the only companies that matter as sort of permanent monopolies,” Andreessen says. “And they’re going to just basically destroy the startup ecosystem underneath that.” Andreessen Horowitz is, of course, invested in that ecosystem, having earmarked $2.25 billion for AI applications and infrastructure. The anti-monopoly rhetoric is in keeping with a16z’s latest marketing push. According to Andreessen’s newsletter, startups are threatened by the government, which is “now far more hostile to new startups than it used to be.” Besides his objections to the way the SEC has increased its oversight of crypto, he is also upset that a stepped-up interest in antitrust has made it more difficult for him to exit investments. “Regulatory agencies are punitively blocking startups from being acquired by the same big companies the government is preferencing in so many other ways,” Andreessen writes. After all, the Federal Trade Commission has launched an inquiry into Big Tech’s partnerships and investments with startups — with the goal of seeing if those partnerships squash competition. The irony is so obvious it’s almost embarrassing to point it out. Andreessen says he is upset that Big Tech is too powerful, but he opposes antitrust action because that blocks a route for VCs to exit. Either you’re comfortable with Big Tech getting bigger, in which case acquisitions are fine, or you want little tech to be competitive, which means blocking industry consolidation. Mainly, it seems that Andreessen believes in cashing out. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz pointedly name Google as a threat to startups. “Google, I think we would all agree, is more powerful than probably 95 percent of countries in the world,” Horowitz says at one point. Google, specifically, is a sore spot with the right wing. Vice presidential nominee Vance has already said it should be broken up. Vance believes Google is controlling information and skewing too far left. Of course, Google’s moderation policies don’t just apply to Google News — they also affect YouTube, which hosts a great many right-wing podcasts without issue. It’s unclear how seriously to take Andreessen and Horowitz’s complaints about Big Tech because the complaints don’t quite square with their behavior. For instance, Facebook is similarly powerful and influential, especially in AI. Andreessen sits on its board. A16z is invested in OpenAI, which has a partnership with Microsoft — and both have lobbied strenuously for more regulation around AI. It sure seems like if a16z wants to change things at those big companies, someone could simply pick up the phone. At this point in the podcast, you could squint and say maybe the concern about AI and crypto is really about technology and progress. But from those two topics, we move on to classic rich guy shit of the most tedious kind: tax reform. Andreessen says it was “the final straw for me. This is the thing that tipped me hard.” They are upset about a proposal to alter capital gains taxes. Capital gains are paid on investment assets, and they are typically paid when the investment is sold and the gains are, in industry terms, “realized.” The new Biden treasury proposal means that for people whose wealth is worth more than $100 million, any unrealized capital gains will be taxed, too. This is what has Andreessen and Horowitz in a tizzy. It means that if they own a clutch of highly valued startup shares, they will have to pay taxes on them before they cash out. This is a “very scary proposal,” Horowitz says. Startups are illiquid assets, Andreessen points out. “Startups never go up and down. They’re never overvalued,” says Horowtiz, dryly. “There’s no bubbles.” Andreessen notes that the way the value of a startup is calculated for the purposes of this proposed tax has to do with the latest round’s valuation. Historically, one of the ways that Andreessen Horowitz has approached startup investing is to inflate a company’s valuation; it is “the OG when it comes to doling out speculative startup valuations.” The new proposed tax punishes this kind of behavior — a high valuation means a high tax. “This makes startups completely implausible,” says Andreessen. “Venture capital just ends. Firms like ours don’t exist.” This is followed by an anxiety spiral that is sort of difficult to convey in text; I suggest you listen for yourself. “California is done,” says Andreessen. “It’s total destruction.” The taxes won’t just target the wealthy; they’ll come for everyone. “Once the structure gets established, the politicians do what they do: they’ll walk the numbers up,” Andreessen says. “Presto chango, we’re Argentina!” says Horowitz. Finally, Horowitz gets ahold of himself. “By the way, this one probably won’t get all the way through the system,” he says. “But it might!” There is another issue that might cause wreckage throughout Silicon Valley. It is immigration. An awful lot of immigrants comprise Silicon Valley’s talent pool — a huge swath of engineers in the US are on H-1B visas. The Trump / Vance ticket is virulently anti-immigrant. The current CEOs of Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and IBM are all immigrants. So are Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates are involved in Fwd.us, a lobbying group dedicated to immigration reform that Musk and Sacks both left. If there were an issue that would rally the people who care most about progress, innovation, and talent, you’d think protecting the immigrants who’ve built lives and careers in tech would be it. Stopping immigration is a core issue of the Trump campaign. During the Republican National Convention, delegates held up signs saying “Mass Deportation Now.” Trump has called the H-1B, the visa many tech workers use to come to Silicon Valley, “very bad” and “unfair” to US workers. In his previous term, he targeted H-1B visa applications specifically; in the fiscal year 2018, almost 25 percent of applications were denied, up from about 13 percent the year before. In fiscal year 2019, 20 percent of H-1B applications were denied. The denials plummeted after several Trump administration rules were thrown out by courts; the denial rate in 2022 was just 2 percent. Immigration plainly matters for crypto — as Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin says, “The crypto industry is uniquely international, and so immigration law is crypto law.” Buterin is one of the most influential voices in crypto, and Ethereum is the foundation for a swath of Andreessen Horowitz’s investment portfolio. Among the investments that rely on it are MakerDAO, VeeFriends, Dapper Labs, and EigenLayer. It is remarkable that the founder of Ethereum is saying that voting for Trump is against the crypto ethos, and the big crypto investors are doing it anyway. The word “immigration” is only mentioned by Andreessen and Horowitz in the podcast when they discuss the rally in which someone attempted an assassination: Trump had turned his head to look at a chart that purported to show illegal immigration into the US as the bullet whizzed by. I wondered why such an important issue for tech wasn’t addressed, so I emailed Margit Wennmachers, a16z’s PR guru, to ask. She didn’t reply. After I finished listening to the podcast, a few things kept nagging at me. Take the very beginning of the podcast. Once upon a time, Andreessen says, you could get very rich and then give the money away in philanthropy, “and you get enormous credit for that. And, you know, it absolves you of whatever.” At some point in the last 10 years, some people suggested that maybe rich people should pay more taxes instead of giving their money away — that perhaps the whims of some random rich person are not the best way to support the most vulnerable in our society. Andreessen and Horowitz suggest that this critique of philanthropy is simply jealousy. It also unbalanced “the deal.” “The deal,” as described on the podcast, is vague. To my ear, it sounds like this: Tech companies could basically do whatever they wanted, as long as people who worked there paid high taxes and donated enough money to charitable causes. The money — taxes, donations — made them the good guys. Andreessen and Horowitz point to the mid-2010s — that is, the era of low interest rates — as the time of “the deal” unraveling. Notably, this is around the time that the tech hype cycle became obvious even to people who weren’t paying attention. This year, it’s scooters! Now it’s viral media companies! Now it’s metaverse! Now it’s crypto! Now it’s AI! These ideas were more or less rejected by the market, except possibly AI. The one thing all these hype cycles had in common was VCs talking their books, as publicly as possible. That charge was led by Andreessen Horowitz. So now, instead of investing in things the market wants, Andreessen and Horowitz appear to be gambling on legislation instead. Their timing is remarkable; not even a week after their Trump endorsement, Biden dropped out of the race, rallying the Democrats behind Vice President Kamala Harris. In the hours immediately following the announcement, small-money donors raised $46.7 million for her campaign. By endorsing Trump, Andreessen and Horowitz have effectively lost whatever leverage they might have had with the Harris campaign. But maybe that doesn’t matter. Near the end of the podcast, Horowitz says that he was shaken by the assassination attempt on Donald Trump because he’s friends with Ivanka, his daughter, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. “Ivanka and the kids were just at my house,” Horowitz says, of learning Trump was shot. “We went to see David Copperfield and all that. So my brain was almost frozen because I had this feeling about, ‘Oh my god, Grandpa just got shot.’” As for Andreessen, he has been inveighing against “woke” capital, engaging in Twitter culture wars, and complaining about what he views as the media’s hostility to free speech for a while now. In Andreessen’s 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” he lists what he terms “patron saints” of the movement. They include Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, an Italian futurist who was also the co-author of The Fascist Manifesto; Nick Land, whose writing is a foundational text for the so-called alt-right; Neven Sesardic, a philosopher who argues that race is biologically real and not socially constructed; and Vilfredo Pareto, who argued that democracy is an illusion. And this talk about democracy brings me to Curtis Yarvin, personal friend of vice presidential candidate Vance. Yarvin, a software developer, is openly anti-democracy. (Yarvin’s recent newsletter, in response to Biden dropping out, enthusiastically advocates for a return to monarchy. Freak shit.) One of Yarvin’s ideas, called “retire all government employees” or RAGE, is part of Project 2025, a Heritage Foundation proposal for what Trump should do if he wins. This rhetoric was echoed by Vance in 2021, who called out Yarvin by name. So this VC cabal is trading against the basic principles of America — not merely against personal freedom, but democracy itself — in the hopes of profit. It’s not the first time tech has made the trade against freedom; IBM made it during the Holocaust. In venture capital, you are what you fund. Andreessen and Horowitz understand this, even embody it. But they aren’t just funding the issues they discuss on their podcast; they are funding Trump and Vance. That means those donations are anti-abortion, anti-immigration, and possibly even anti-democracy because that is what the Trump / Vance ticket stands for. These are not subsidiary issues: these are now what two of Silicon Valley’s most prominent figures now stand for, too. Is that a good investment? articles.title: ”Trump beter sig som en rysk allierad”
articles.summary: Trump ”hyllar Putin så mycket” och uttalar sig allt hårdare om Zelenskyj. Experter anklagar Trump för att ”bete sig som en rysk allierad”, enligt VG.
articles.body_text: Trump ”hyllar Putin så mycket” samtidigt som han uttalar sig allt hårdare om Zelenskyj, säger experter till norska VG . – Trump beter sig som en rysk allierad, säger USA-experten Eirik Løkke. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Donald Trump tillkännagav nyligen att han ingått ett dieselavtal med Ryssland. Under fredagen kom beskedet att Ryssland och USA diskuterar en rad nya gemensamma projekt, skriver Independent . Trump har också trappat upp tonläget mot ukrainske presidenten Volodymyr Zelenskyj och sagt att Ukraina ”behöver en ny ledare”. – Jag tycker att Zelenskyj är svårare att ha att göra med än Putin, sade Trump till tv-kanalen Newsmax tidigare i veckan. Trump kallade också Ukrainas attacker mot ryska oljeanläggningar för ”en skam”. – Det är på flera sätt obegripligt att Trump hyllar Putin så mycket, säger USA -experten Eirik Løkke. Iver B Neumann, forskare i internationell politik, säger att Trumps beteende försätter Zelenskyj i en svår situation. – Zelenskyj har låtit sig förödmjukas av USA eftersom Ukraina är beroende av amerikanskt stöd. Men om de förödmjukas för länge framstår de som svaga, och då är det slut med dem, säger Neumann. Det har i veckan rapporterats om amerikanska restriktioner för satellitsystemet Starlink som är viktigt för Ukrainas försvar. Løkke tror att restriktionerna kan vara ett försök att pressa Zelenskyj att acceptera ett fredsavtal på Trumps villkor. Løkke varnar för att minskat amerikanskt stöd ”tippar krigsbalansen till Rysslands fördel”. Neumann anser att Europa måste ta större ansvar för kontinentens trygghet nu när det amerikanska stödet till Ukraina ifrågasätts.

articles.summary: ”Blå tunna-mordet” skakade hela landet. Nu har en kvinna och hennes pojkvän dömts till döden för mordet.
articles.body_text: ”Blå tunnan-mordet” skakade hela landet, enligt People. Nu har en kvinna och hennes pojkvän dömts till döden för det ”ohyggliga” mordet, skriver NDTV. Kvinnan har fött ett barn under tiden hon suttit fängslad. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Indiskan Muskan Rastogi gifte sig med maken Saurabh Rajput 2016. Fem år senare inledde hon en affär med sin tidigare klasskamrat Sahil Shukla, enligt BBC . När Rajput fick reda på att hans fru var otrogen ville han skilja sig, men släktingar försökte övertala honom att ändra sig eftersom paret hade ett ungt barn. Den 3 mars förra året befann sig Rajput i indiska staden Meerut. Han fick då mat som innehöll lugnande medel av Rastogi. Sedan dödades han av Rastogi och Shukla som styckade kroppen, enligt polisen. Rajputs kropp hittades 15 dagar senare i en stor blå plastbehållare vilket ledde till att fallet kallades ”blå tunnan-mordet” i medierna. Rastogi och Shukla greps och ställdes inför rätta för mordet. De befanns skyldiga i slutet av förra månaden. När påföljden meddelades i veckan dömdes paret till döden. Både 26-åriga Rastogi, som fött ett barn under tiden hon suttit fängslad, och 28-åriga Shukla ”grät okontrollerat” efter dödsdomen, enligt NDTV. – Min bror dödades av grymma människor, säger Rajputs bror till BBC. articles.title: Gåtan om Patricia löst – efter 36 år
articles.summary: En kvinna hittades död – men ingen visste vem hon var. 36 år senare har mysteriet lösts.
articles.body_text: En kvinna hittades död – men ingen visste vem hon var. 36 år senare har mysteriet lösts, skriver People . ”Hon har väntat alldeles för länge på att bli identifierad”, skriver polisen om fyrbarnsmamman. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Den 23 juli 1990 ryckte räddningstjänsten ut efter larm om en bilolycka på en motorväg i södra Kalifornien. Då hittade man en kvinnas kvarlevor 18 meter nerför en sluttning intill vägen. När man genomsökte området hittades fler skelettdelar, fem tänder, en hårborste, tygbitar och ett metallspänne, enligt polisen. Men kvinnan som hittats kunde ändå inte identifieras. Och så skulle det bli förbli i 36 år – fram tills nu. Förra året inledde polisen ett samarbete med ett företag specialiserat på rättsgenetisk släktforskning – och det gav resultat. Polisen har nu tillkännagett att kvinnan vars kvarlevor hittades intill motorvägen för 36 år sedan var fyrbarnsmamman Patricia Diana Hunt Fielding som föddes 1933. ”Även om hennes identitet nu är känd förblir mycket om Patricias liv och omständigheterna kring hennes död ett mysterium”, skriver polisen som vädjar till allmänheten om hjälp. Alla som har information om Fielding uppmanas att kontakta polisen som hoppas få fram information om ”var hon befann sig innan hennes kvarlevor upptäcktes och vad som hände henne”. ”Trots att årtionden gått är det aldrig för sent att hjälpa till att ge hennes familj svar, precis som det inte var för sent att ge namnet tillbaka till någon som har väntat alldeles för länge på att bli identifierad”, skriver polisen.
